FastQA shows a slight increase of   $2.2\%/3.2\%$   for W IKI H OP and a decrease of   $2.7\%/4.1\%$   on M ED H OP . While inconclusive, it is clear that  FastQA  with fewer la- tent interactions than    $B i D A F$   has problems integrat- ing cross-document information.

The TF-IDF retrieval baseline clearly performs better than random for W IKI H OP , but is not very strong overall. That is, the question tokens are help- ful to detect relevant documents, but exploiting only this information compares poorly to the other base- lines. On the other hand, as no co-mention of an interacting drug pair occurs within any single doc- ument in M ED H OP , the TF-IDF baseline performs worse than random. We conclude that lexical match- ing with a single support document is not enough to build a strong predictive model for both datasets.

Extractive RC models: FastQA and BiDAF In our experiments we evaluate two recently proposed LSTM -based extractive QA models: the Bidirec- tional Attention Flow model   $(B i D A F$  , Seo et al. (2017a)), and  FastQA  (Weissenborn et al., 2017), which have shown a robust performance across sev- eral datasets. These models predict an answer span within a  single  document. We adapt them to a multi- document setting by sequentially concatenating all  $d\ \in\ S_{q}$   in random order into a superdocument, adding document separator tokens. During training, the ﬁrst answer mention in the concatenated docu- ment serves as the gold span.   At test time, we mea- sured accuracy based on the exact match between the prediction and answer, both lowercased, after re- moving articles, trailing white spaces and punctu- ation, in the same way as Rajpurkar et al. (2016). To rule out any signal stemming from the order of documents in the superdocument, this order is ran- domized both at training and test time. In a prelimi- nary experiment we also trained models using differ- ent random document order permutations, but found that performance did not change signiﬁcantly.

The  Document-cue  baseline can predict more than a third of the samples correctly, for both datasets, even after sub-sampling frequent document-answer pairs for W IKI H OP . The relative strength of this and other baselines proves to be an important is- sue when designing multi-hop datasets, which we addressed through the measures described in Sec- tion 3.2. In Table 4 we compare the two relevant baselines on W IKI H OP  before and after applying ﬁltering measures. The absolute strength of these baselines before ﬁltering shows how vital address- ing this issue is:   $74.6\%$   accuracy could be reached through exploiting the  cooccurrence  $(d,c)$   statistic alone. This underlines the paramount importance of investigating and addressing dataset biases that oth- erwise would confound seemingly strong RC model performance. The relative drop demonstrates that

Among the two neural models,  $B i D A F$   is overall strongest across both datasets – this is in contrast to the reported results for SQuAD where their perfor- mance is nearly indistinguishable. This is possibly due to the iterative latent interactions in the    $B i D A F$  architecture: we hypothesize that these are of in- creased importance for our task, where information is distributed across documents. It is worth empha- sizing that unlike the other baselines, both  FastQA and  $B i D A F$   predict the answer by extracting a span from the support documents without relying on the candidate options    $C_{q}$  .

Related Datasets End-to-end text-based QA has witnessed a surge in interest with the advent of large- scale datasets, which have been assembled based on F REEBASE  (Berant et al., 2013; Bordes et al., 2015), W IKIPEDIA  (Yang et al., 2015; Rajpurkar et al., 2016; Hewlett et al., 2016), web search queries (Nguyen et al., 2016), news articles (Her- mann et al., 2015; Onishi et al., 2016), books (Hill et al., 2016; Paperno et al., 2016), science ex- ams (Welbl et al., 2017), and trivia (Boyd-Graber et al., 2012; Dunn et al., 2017). Besides  Trivi- aQA  (Joshi et al., 2017), all these datasets are con- ﬁned to single documents, and RC typically does not require a combination of multiple independent facts. In contrast, W IKI H OP  and M ED H OP  are speciﬁ- cally designed for cross-document RC and multi- step inference. There exist other multi-hop RC re- sources, but they are either very limited in size, such as the  FraCaS  test suite, or based on synthetic language (Weston et al., 2016). TriviaQA  partly involves multi-step reasoning, but the complexity largely stems from parsing compositional questions. Our datasets center around compositional inference from comparatively simple queries and the cross- document setup ensures that multi-step inference goes beyond resolving co-reference.

Both neural RC models are able to largely retain or even improve their strong performance when an- swers are masked: they are able to leverage the tex- tual context of the candidate expressions. To under- stand differences in model behavior between W IK - I H OP  and M ED H OP , it is worth noting that drug mentions in M ED H OP  are normalized to a unique single-word identiﬁer, and performance drops under masking. In contrast, for the open-domain setting of W IKI H OP , a reduction of the answer vocabulary to 100 random single-token  mask  expressions clearly helps the model in selecting a candidate span, com- pared to the multi-token candidate expressions in the unmasked setting. Overall, although both neural RC models clearly outperform the other baselines, they still have large room for improvement compared to human performance at  $74\%\,/\,85\%$   for W IKI H OP .

For both datasets we then establish several strong baselines and evaluate the performance of two pre- viously proposed competitive RC models (Seo et al., 2017a; Weissenborn et al., 2017). We ﬁnd that one can integrate information across documents, but nei- ther excels at selecting relevant information from a larger documents set, as their accuracy increases sig- niﬁcantly when given only documents guaranteed to be relevant. The best model reaches   $54.5\%$   on an annotated test set, compared to human performance at  $85.0\%$  , indicating ample room for improvement.

question: How do different configurations of positional encodings and loss components affect Average Precision (AP) in the DETR-DC5 model for object detection?
answer:
Based on the provided context, different configurations of positional encodings and loss components significantly affect the Average Precision (AP) in the DETR-DC5 model for object detection. Here's a detailed breakdown:

### Positional Encodings

1. **No Spatial Positional Encodings:**
   - When spatial positional encodings are completely removed, the model still achieves an AP of more than 32, which is a drop of 7.8 AP compared to the baseline model that uses fixed sine positional encodings passed at every attention layer.

2. **Fixed Sine Spatial Positional Encodings:**
   - Passing fixed sine spatial positional encodings along with output positional encodings at input leads to a 1.4 AP drop compared to passing positional encodings directly in attention layers.

3. **Learned Spatial Encodings:**
   - Using learned spatial encodings passed to the attentions gives similar results to fixed sine encodings, indicating that the model can adapt to learned embeddings effectively.

4. **No Spatial Encodings in Encoder:**
   - Not passing any spatial encodings in the encoder only leads to a minor AP drop of 1.3 AP, suggesting that the encoder's role in disentangling objects might be less critical when other components compensate.

5. **Shared Across All Layers:**
   - When spatial positional encodings are passed to the attentions, they are shared across all layers, and the output encodings (object queries) are always learned, ensuring consistency in how the model processes information.

### Loss Components

1. **Classiﬁcation Loss:**
   - This is essential for training and cannot be turned off. It ensures that the model learns to correctly classify objects.

2. **Bounding Box Distance Loss:**
   - Training a model without this loss component shows a significant drop in performance, highlighting its importance in accurately predicting bounding box coordinates.

3. **GIoU Loss:**
   - The GIoU loss, when used alone, accounts for a substantial portion of the improvement in AP. It helps in better alignment of predicted bounding boxes with ground truth, especially for overlapping objects.

### Combined Effects

- **Baseline Model:**
  - The baseline model uses fixed sine positional encodings passed at every attention layer in both the encoder and decoder, achieving an AP of 39.2.

- **Model Without Bounding Box Distance Loss:**
  - This model shows a drop in AP, emphasizing the need for accurate bounding box predictions.

- **Model Without GIoU Loss:**
  - Similarly, this model also shows a drop in AP, indicating the importance of GIoU in improving the quality of bounding box predictions.

### Conclusion

The context reveals that both positional encodings and loss components play crucial roles in the performance of the DETR-DC5 model. While the model can function with minimal positional encodings, the inclusion of appropriate encodings and loss functions significantly enhances its ability to detect objects accurately. Specifically, the combination of fixed sine positional encodings and the use of GIoU loss contributes to the highest AP scores, demonstrating the synergy between these components in optimizing object detection performance.

question: How does the ProgramFC model compare to FLAN-T5 in terms of F1 scores across different model sizes and task complexities, and what are the observed retrieval recall differences between ProgramFC and one-step retrieval?
answer:
Based on the provided context, here's a comprehensive answer to your question:

### Comparison of ProgramFC and FLAN-T5 in Terms of F1 Scores

question: How does ProgramFC's performance compare with other models across different fact-checking tasks, and what are the error trends in its predictions?
answer:
ProgramFC demonstrates superior performance across various fact-checking tasks compared to other models. In terms of error trends, the primary sources of errors in ProgramFC's predictions are Reasoning Error and Retrieval Augmentation (RAG) Error. StepBack Error is relatively low at 0.01, suggesting that the step-back prompting technique effectively mitigates some errors. Scoring Error is negligible at 0.02, implying that the model's scoring mechanism is quite accurate.

Overall, ProgramFC balances model capability, learning efficiency, and interpretability, making it a robust choice for fact-checking complex claims. Its ability to generate reasoning programs provides clear explanations of its reasoning process, enhancing both its reliability and user trust. However, addressing the dominant sources of errors, particularly in reasoning and retrieval, remains an important area for future improvement.

question: How do error types and model performance vary across 2-hop, 3-hop, and 4-hop scenarios in HOVER and FEVEROUS datasets?
answer:
Based on the provided context, we can analyze how error types and model performance vary across 2-hop, 3-hop, and 4-hop scenarios in the HOVER and FEVEROUS datasets.

### Error Types

1. **Reasoning Error (R):**
   - This error type occurs when the retrieved context is relevant, but the model still fails to reason through the context to arrive at the right answer.
   - In the 2-hop scenario, Reasoning Error is less prevalent compared to higher hops.
   - As the complexity increases to 3-hop and 4-hop, Reasoning Error becomes more significant, indicating that models struggle more with multi-step reasoning.

2. **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Error:**
   - RAG Error involves issues where the model retrieves incorrect or insufficient information to generate a correct answer.
   - Similar to Reasoning Error, RAG Error increases with the number of hops, showing that models have difficulty retrieving the necessary information for complex reasoning tasks.

3. **StepBack Error:**
   - StepBack Error is associated with the failure of the StepBack method to correctly guide the reasoning process.
   - This error type is relatively low in 2-hop scenarios but increases as the reasoning depth increases, suggesting that StepBack becomes less effective with more complex reasoning tasks.

### Model Performance

1. **Performance Trends:**
   - The performance of models generally decreases as the number of reasoning hops increases. This trend is evident in both the HOVER and FEVEROUS datasets.
   - For instance, in the HOVER dataset, models perform better on 2-hop claims compared to 3-hop and 4-hop claims. The same pattern is observed in the FEVEROUS dataset.

2. **Specific Models:**
   - **GPT-4:** Shows superior performance on 2-hop reasoning tasks compared to other models. However, its performance degrades as the number of hops increases.
   - **PaLM-2L + Step-Back:** This combination shows improved performance over direct prompting methods, especially in 2-hop scenarios. It also performs better than other models on 3-hop and 4-hop tasks, indicating the effectiveness of incorporating logical constraints and step-back reasoning.

3. **Aggregating Reasoning Programs:**
   - Aggregating the predictions of multiple reasoning programs improves performance over using a single program. This approach yields an average improvement of 1.5% in performance across different hop lengths.

### Conclusion

In summary, as the reasoning depth increases from 2-hop to 4-hop, both error types and model performance show a clear trend:
- **Error Types:** Reasoning Error, RAG Error, and StepBack Error increase, reflecting the growing complexity and challenges in multi-hop reasoning.
- **Model Performance:** Models generally perform better on simpler 2-hop tasks and struggle more with 3-hop and 4-hop tasks, highlighting the need for more sophisticated reasoning strategies and logical constraints to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks.

This analysis underscores the importance of developing methods that can handle multi-hop reasoning effectively, such as incorporating logical constraints and aggregating reasoning programs, to enhance the performance of large language models on complex fact-checking tasks.

question: How does the 'hard-to-contrast' strategy perform compared to other querying strategies across different datasets, and how does it influence the initial query selection?
answer:
The 'hard-to-contrast' strategy performs exceptionally well compared to other querying strategies across various datasets, including PathMNIST, OrganAMNIST, BloodMNIST, and CIFAR-10-LT. This strategy significantly outperforms random selection and several other active querying methods, such as BALD, Margin, VAAL, Entropy, and Coreset. For instance, on PathMNIST, OrganAMNIST, and BloodMNIST, the hard-to-contrast strategy achieves improvements of 1.8%, 2.6%, and 5.2% respectively when querying only 0.1% of the dataset.

In terms of initial query selection, the 'hard-to-contrast' strategy is particularly effective because it is label-free and can select data that represent the most common patterns in the entire dataset. This approach helps alleviate the cold start problem in vision active learning by ensuring that the initial queries are more representative and diverse. The strategy integrates K-means clustering with contrastive features, which allows it to cover a broader range of classes, including those that are less frequent or harder to learn. As a result, it achieves better class coverage and performance, even at low budget scenarios.

Overall, the 'hard-to-contrast' strategy not only surpasses random selection but also outperforms other active querying strategies, making it a strong baseline for initial query selection in image classification tasks.

question: How do different instruction formats and demonstration selections impact the performance of ChatGPT and Codex on the FewNERD dataset, and how does this compare with other models?
answer:

### Impact of Different Instruction Formats and Demonstration Selections on ChatGPT and Codex Performance

1. **Instruction Formats:**
   - The context discusses various instruction formats used in multimodal models, particularly focusing on how these formats impact performance. For instance, simple instructions (like I1) are often more effective than complex ones for tasks like Named Entity Recognition (NER). 2. **Demonstration Selections:**
   - In-context few-shot learning is a technique where models use examples at inference time to understand and perform tasks. The selection of these examples is crucial. The context notes that while in-context examples can enhance performance, they must align perfectly with the format of the inference query, making them complex and lengthy to incorporate.
   - The cold-start strategy mentioned in the context involves collecting in-context examples using system messages and visual annotations before large-scale queries. This approach helps in identifying satisfactory examples that can effectively guide the model.

3. **Performance on FewNERD Dataset:**
   - The FewNERD dataset is a fine-grained NER dataset, and the context provides insights into how different models perform on it. ### Conclusion

In summary, the format of instructions and the selection of demonstrations play a critical role in the performance of models like ChatGPT and Codex. Simple and multimodal instructions tend to yield better results, especially for tasks requiring clear and concise guidance. While these models show promise, particularly in tasks like NER and EAE, they face challenges with fine-grained datasets like FewNERD. question: What are the most common reasoning steps and challenges encountered when verifying claims in the SciTAB dataset?
answer:
Based on the provided context, the most common reasoning steps and challenges encountered when verifying claims in the SciTAB dataset include:

1. **Reasoning Steps:**
   - **Simple Lookup:** Retrieving specific values from a table, which accounts for about 20.6% of the reasoning steps.
   - **Compositional Reasoning:** This involves combining multiple pieces of information from the table to draw conclusions. The average reasoning depth for claims is 4.76 steps, with some claims requiring up to 11 steps.
   - **Commonsense Knowledge:** Applying general knowledge to interpret or verify claims that are not directly stated in the table.
   - **Numerical Reasoning:** Involves calculations or comparisons based on numerical data presented in the tables.

2. **Challenges:**
   - **Table Grounding:** Ensuring that the reasoning process correctly interprets the data within the table context.
   - **Ambiguous Claims:** Handling claims that are vague or lack clarity, often due to pronouns or incomplete sentences.
   - **Compositional Reasoning:** Verifying claims that require integrating multiple types of domain knowledge and reasoning steps.
   - **Not Enough Info (NEI) Claims:** Identifying claims that cannot be verified solely based on the table data, requiring additional background knowledge or external sources.
   - **Refuted Claims:** Verifying claims that are contradicted by the evidence in the table, which requires careful analysis to ensure accuracy.

The SciTAB dataset is designed to address these challenges by providing a comprehensive set of claims that require varied and complex reasoning processes, making it a valuable resource for evaluating and improving automated fact-checking systems in scientific contexts.

Our data is derived from the Sci- Gen dataset ( Moosavi et al. ,  2021 ), a resource that includes scientific tables and claims crawled from arXiv.org. We first manually filter out the check- worthy scientific claims from the raw data. Follow- ing this, we employ a strategy of human–model collaboration, as depicted in Figure  2 , to generate claims that are either contradicted or un verifiable based on the table’s content. Figure  1  shows a claim from S CI T AB  and the corresponding reason- ing process to verify it. Compared with existing benchmarks, S CI T AB  is closer to real-world scien- tific fact-checking in terms of more realistic claims and table-based evidence. Through data analysis, we further show that the claims in S CI T AB  neces- sitate a more comprehensive and nuanced set of reasoning skills for verification,  e.g.,  numerical rea-

Closed Source LLMs. These are closed-source LLMs that require API calls for inference, includ- ing  Instruct GP T (text-davinci-003)  ( Ouyang et al. ,  2022 ) and  GPT-4  ( OpenAI ,  2023 ). We evaluate the setting that directly predicts the la- bel and the  Chain-of-Thought  (CoT) ( Wei et al. , 2022 ) setting, which generates explanations be- fore predicting the final label. We also include the Program-of-Thoughts  (PoT) ( Chen et al. ,  2022 ) model that has shown strong ability in solving com- plex numerical reasoning tasks. It first parses the reasoning steps as Python programs and then exe- cutes them on a Python interpreter to derive accu- rate answers. Since most claims in S CI T AB  also re- quire numerical reasoning, we want to test whether program-guided reasoning can be extended to table- based fact-checking.

The dataset was created by crawling computer sci- ence papers from arXiv. The tables and the texts explaining the tables are extracted from the papers to create (table, description) pairs for the task of data-to-text generation. From all the table descrip- tions of SciGen, we first filter the check-worthy scientific claims following the criteria established by  Lee et al.  ( 2009 ) for academic writing 1 . We focus on the descriptions that serve the purpose of “highlighting and commenting on key data”, i.e. , describing research findings based on the data presented in scientific tables. Given the task’s ob- jective nature and to save the cost of human labor, we hire a graduate student majoring in computer science to manually select scientific claims based on the aforementioned criteria using the user inter- face in Appendix  A.2 . This decision was based on a pilot annotation which showed that a well-trained annotator can achieve over   $95\%$   accuracy in filter- ing scientific claims. To safeguard the quality, we include an option to mark the claim as “Discard-It’s not a claim, or it’s an incomplete, or not grammat- ically correct sentence.” during the subsequent claim verification process. Using this approach, we filtered out 872 real-world scientific claims from 1,301 table descriptions in the SciGen dataset.

One potential risk of model-generated claims is that they may lack diversity and exhibit the same pattern. For example, in the Sci-Fact ( Wadden et al. ,  2020 ) dataset where the refuted claims are generated by flapping the meaning of the original true claims, we found that out of 100 randomly sampled refuted claims, 85 simply negated the orig- inal claim by adding negation words such as “not” (more details in Appendix  C ). To evaluate the diver- sity of claims for our S CI T AB  dataset, we randomly select 60 refuted claims and then manually anno- tate their reasons for refutation. Results are shown in Table  3  (top half). We find that S CI T AB  exhibits a greater diversity in refuted claims compared to Sci-Fact. Besides common error types such as “in- correct calculation results”   $(41.7\%)$  , there are also unique types of errors that are more reflective of the complexities in real-world scientific claims. For example,   $33.33\%$   of the refuted claims contain “in- correct approximation words”, and   $10.0\%$   are cases where “the claim is partially right”, consistent with the fact that ambiguity and half-truths are common phenomena in scientific discourse. Additional ex- amples of refuted claims are in Appendix  E .

We present S CI T AB , a novel dataset for scien- tific fact-checking that addresses the limitations of existing benchmarks. By incorporating real- world scientific claims and their corresponding evidence in the form of tables, S CI T AB  offers a more comprehensive and fine-grained representa- tion of scientific reasoning. The challenging nature of S CI T AB  is evident from the performance of the state-of-the-art, highlighting the need for further research. For example, we believe that addressing the challenges posed by ambiguous claims repre- sents a crucial direction for research in scientific fact-checking ( Glockner et al. ,  2023 ;  Liu et al. , 2023a ). One potential approach is to enhance the disambiguation of ambiguous claims by leverag- ing contextual information or external knowledge sources. Additionally, studying the compositional- ity in table-based reasoning is an interesting direc- tion. Consider the work of Self-Ask ( Press et al. , 2022 ), which proposed the “compositional it y gap” metric to measure the capability of LLMs in com- positional reasoning. Such evaluations can be en- riched by annotating S CI T AB  with ground-truth reasoning depths and structured reasoning graphs. Beyond this, another direction worth exploring is equipping the LLMs with external tools to further improve the model. For example, the use of GPT- 4 plugins, Program-guided Fact-Checking ( Pan et al. ,  2023 ) or adopting approaches from other tool- augmented LLMs like Toolformer ( Schick et al. , 2023 ) and Chameleon ( Lu et al. ,  2023 ).

Reasoning Types. To study the nature of reason- ing involved in fact-checking claims in S CI T AB , we adapt the set of table-based reasoning cate- gories from INFOTABS ( Gupta et al. ,  2020 ) to define 14 atomic reasoning types, as shown in Ta- ble  2 . Among them, “closed-domain knowledge” and “open-domain knowledge” are specially de- signed for S CI T AB . Closed-domain knowledge refers to obtaining background information from the table caption or title,  e.g. , knowing that “Prod.” refers to “Productivity” from the table caption in Figure  1 . Open-domain knowledge refers to com- monsense knowledge not presented in the table, e.g. , the relationship between precision and recall. Given the designed reasoning types, we manually analyze 100 samples in S CI T AB , by annotating the graph of reasoning steps for verifying each claim. We identify 476 atomic reasoning steps from the 100 analyzed samples and show the proportion for each reasoning type in Table  2 . We observe that S C - I T AB  has a multifaceted complex range of reason- ing types and a high proportion of claims requiring different types of domain knowledge.

question: What are the main reasoning functions and their usage proportions in the SciTab dataset, and how does this relate to the complexity of reasoning steps required?
answer:
Based on the provided context, particularly from Document 12 and Document 13, we can outline the main reasoning functions and their usage proportions in the SciTab dataset:

1. **Add (Calculate the sum of two numbers)**: This function has a proportion of 4.0%. It involves basic arithmetic operations to verify claims that require simple addition.

2. **Max / Min**: This function is used for retrieving the maximum or minimum number from a set of numbers and has a proportion of 3.1%. It is crucial for claims that involve identifying extremes within a dataset.

3. **Col / Rowname**: Retrieving column or row names from the table is necessary for claims that require specific references to data columns or rows. This function has a proportion of 3.1%.

4. **Trend same/different**: Determining whether trends for two columns or rows are the same or different is important for analyzing patterns over time or across categories. This function has a proportion of 2.9%.

5. **Set check**: Verifying if a value belongs to a set of numbers is essential for claims that involve membership checks within a defined set. This function also has a proportion of 2.9%.

These reasoning functions collectively highlight the multifaceted nature of reasoning required in the SciTab dataset. The presence of these diverse functions indicates that the dataset demands a complex array of reasoning steps to accurately verify claims. For instance, a claim might require not only identifying the maximum value in a dataset but also comparing trends between different columns to fully understand the implications of the data presented.

The complexity of reasoning steps required is further evidenced by the fact that claims in the SciTab dataset often necessitate multiple reasoning steps. For example, verifying a claim might involve first calculating a sum, then determining the trend of the resulting values, and finally checking if these values belong to a specific set. This multi-step process underscores the sophisticated reasoning capabilities needed to effectively evaluate claims in the SciTab dataset.

In summary, the SciTab dataset's reasoning functions and their proportions reflect a high level of complexity, requiring a combination of basic arithmetic, pattern recognition, and set membership verification to accurately assess scientific claims based on tabular data.

question: What are the main reasoning types and their proportions in the ScITab dataset, and how do they relate to the distribution of reasoning steps and common error types?
answer:
Based on the provided context, here's a comprehensive answer to your question regarding the reasoning types and their proportions in the ScITab dataset, along with their relation to the distribution of reasoning steps and common error types:

### Main Reasoning Types and Their Proportions

The ScITab dataset encompasses a multifaceted range of reasoning types, each contributing uniquely to the complexity of verifying scientific claims. The primary reasoning types identified include:

1. **Simple Lookup**: This involves retrieving specific values directly from the data presented in scientific tables. It is the most straightforward type of reasoning and constitutes a significant portion of the dataset, reflecting its foundational role in fact-checking.

2. **Numerical Reasoning**: This type requires understanding and manipulating numerical data, often involving calculations or comparisons. It is crucial for claims that involve quantitative analysis and forms a substantial part of the dataset.

3. **Commonsense Knowledge**: This reasoning type relies on general knowledge and logical deductions that are not explicitly stated in the data. It is essential for interpreting implicit information and contributes significantly to the dataset's complexity.

4. **Domain Knowledge**: This involves specialized knowledge relevant to the scientific field under consideration. It is necessary for claims that require an understanding of specific scientific concepts and theories, making it a critical component of the dataset.

5. **Compositional Reasoning**: This type combines multiple reasoning steps to address complex claims that require integrating various pieces of information. It is particularly challenging and represents a smaller but significant portion of the dataset.

### Distribution of Reasoning Steps

The distribution of reasoning steps in the ScITab dataset reveals the varying levels of complexity involved in verifying claims:

- **Shallow Claims (1–2 Reasoning Steps)**: These are highlighted in red and represent simpler claims that can be verified with minimal reasoning. They form a smaller portion of the dataset but are essential for establishing baseline verification capabilities.

- **Deep Claims (3+ Reasoning Steps)**: Highlighted in blue, these claims require more complex reasoning processes, often involving multiple steps and types of reasoning. They constitute a larger portion of the dataset and reflect the dataset's focus on challenging and multifaceted claims.

### Common Error Types

The analysis of error types in the ScITab dataset provides insights into the challenges faced by models in accurately verifying claims:

1. **Reasoning Error**: This is the most prevalent error type, indicating issues in the logical flow or integration of reasoning steps. It underscores the need for models to handle complex, compositional reasoning effectively.

2. **RAG Error**: Retrieval-Augmentation Generation errors occur when models fail to retrieve or integrate relevant information from external sources. This highlights the importance of robust retrieval mechanisms in enhancing model performance.

3. **StepBack Error**: This error type relates to the failure to step back and consider broader contexts or alternative interpretations. It emphasizes the need for models to incorporate higher-level reasoning and contextual understanding.

4. **Scoring Error**: While less frequent, scoring errors indicate issues in the evaluation of claim veracity. This suggests the need for more accurate and nuanced scoring mechanisms.

### Conclusion

The ScITab dataset presents a comprehensive and challenging benchmark for evaluating models' ability to reason over scientific claims. The diverse reasoning types and their proportions, along with the distribution of reasoning steps and common error types, highlight the dataset's focus on capturing the complexity and variety of scientific reasoning. By addressing these challenges, researchers can develop more sophisticated models capable of handling the intricate demands of scientific fact-checking.

question: What are the primary reasons for refuted claims in the SciTab dataset, and how do different large language models perform in fact-checking these claims in zero-shot and in-context settings?
answer:
Based on the provided context, here is a comprehensive answer to your question:

### Primary Reasons for Refuted Claims in the SciTab Dataset

The SciTab dataset contains refuted claims that are primarily generated by altering the original true claims, often through negation or other forms of modification. The analysis of these refuted claims reveals several key reasons for their refutation:

1. **Incorrect Calculation Results**: A significant portion (41.7%) of the refuted claims involve incorrect calculations or approximations. This indicates that numerical reasoning errors are a common reason for claims being refuted.

2. **Inaccurate Approximation Words**: Approximately 33.33% of the refuted claims contain words that inaccurately approximate values or relationships. This suggests that ambiguity in language can lead to claims being refuted.

3. **Partially Right Claims**: About 10.0% of the refuted claims are partially correct but still considered inaccurate due to incomplete or misleading information.

4. **Insufficient Evidence**: Many refuted claims lack sufficient evidence within the table or the surrounding context to support their validity.

5. **Ambiguous Claims**: Some claims are inherently ambiguous, making it difficult to determine their accuracy without additional context or clarification.

6. **Misinterpretation of Data**: Errors in interpreting the data presented in the tables can also lead to refuted claims.

### Performance of Large Language Models in Fact-Checking These Claims

The performance of large language models (LLMs) in fact-checking these claims varies depending on whether they are evaluated in zero-shot or in-context settings:

1. **Zero-Shot Settings**:
   - **GPT-turbo**: Shows a moderate level of performance but struggles with complex reasoning tasks.
   - **Text-davinci-003**: Performs better than GPT-turbo, demonstrating improved reasoning capabilities.
   - **GPT-4**: Exhibits superior performance, handling complex reasoning tasks more effectively.
   - **Vicuna-13B and Llama2-13B**: These models show varying levels of performance, with Vicuna-13B generally performing better than Llama2-13B.

2. **In-Context Settings**:
   - In in-context settings, where models are provided with additional context or examples, their performance improves significantly.
   - **GPT-4** continues to outperform other models, showing robustness in handling complex reasoning tasks even with limited context.
   - **Text-davinci-003** also shows improved performance, benefiting from the additional context provided.
   - **Vicuna-13B and Llama2-13B** show moderate improvements, but their performance remains less consistent compared to GPT-4 and Text-davinci-003.

### Conclusion

The primary reasons for refuted claims in the SciTab dataset include incorrect calculations, inaccurate approximation words, partially right claims, insufficient evidence, ambiguous claims, and misinterpretation of data. Large language models exhibit varying levels of performance in fact-checking these claims, with GPT-4 consistently outperforming other models, especially in handling complex reasoning tasks. In-context settings generally improve model performance, highlighting the importance of providing additional context for accurate fact-checking.

question: What are the primary reasons for refuted and NEI claims in ScITaB, and how do these reasons impact the performance of different models in zero-shot 3-class classification?
answer:
In the SCITAB dataset, refuted and NEI (Not Enough Information) claims are primarily driven by several key factors that impact model performance in zero-shot 3-class classification tasks. These reasons include:

1. **Insufficient Evidence in Tables**: Many refuted claims lack sufficient evidence within the provided tables to support their validity. This deficiency makes it challenging for models to accurately verify such claims without additional context.

2. **Lack of Background Knowledge**: Both refuted and NEI claims often require external knowledge beyond what is available in the table. The absence of this knowledge can lead to misclassification, as models may not have the necessary information to make informed decisions.

3. **Ambiguity in Claims**: Some claims are inherently ambiguous, making it difficult to determine whether they are supported, refuted, or unverifiable based solely on the given data. This ambiguity is particularly prevalent in NEI cases.

4. **Complex Reasoning Requirements**: Refuted claims frequently involve complex reasoning steps that go beyond simple fact-checking. Models must perform multiple reasoning steps to arrive at a conclusion, which is a significant challenge in zero-shot settings.

5. **Domain-Specific Knowledge**: The need for domain-specific knowledge is another critical factor. Many claims require understanding of specific scientific concepts or methodologies, which may not be adequately captured by general-purpose language models.

These factors collectively contribute to the difficulty models face in accurately classifying claims into the three categories (supported, refuted, NEI). The inclusion of the NEI class, in particular, tends to reduce model confidence, leading to a higher tendency to default to "NEI" when faced with uncertain or complex claims. This behavior is evident in the results where models show poorer performance in the 3-class setting compared to the 2-class setting, highlighting the challenges posed by the NEI class.

Overall, the complexity and variety of reasoning involved in SCITAB make it a more comprehensive and realistic representation of the challenges faced in real-world scientific fact-checking, thus serving as a robust benchmark for evaluating the capabilities of current models in handling nuanced and complex claims.

question: Compare the performance of InstructGPT and GPT-4 on the zero-shot 3-class classification task and analyze the types of errors that contribute to their performance differences.
answer:
Based on the provided context, particularly Document 1 and Context image 4 (Figure 4), we can compare the performance of InstructGPT and GPT-4 on the zero-shot 3-class classification task and analyze the types of errors contributing to their performance differences.

### Performance Comparison:
1. **InstructGPT**:
   - InstructGPT struggles significantly with accurately predicting the NEI (Not Enough Information) class.
   - It frequently misclassifies supported and refuted claims as NEI, indicating a lack of confidence in its predictions for these classes.
   - The confusion matrix in Figure 4 shows that InstructGPT has a higher proportion of misclassifications in the NEI category compared to GPT-4.

2. **GPT-4**:
   - GPT-4 also faces challenges with the NEI class but exhibits a different pattern of errors.
   - Unlike InstructGPT, GPT-4 tends to overclassify NEI claims as either supported or refuted, showing overconfidence in its predictions.
   - The confusion matrix for GPT-4 in Figure 4 reveals a higher rate of misclassification in the NEI category, but the pattern is distinct from InstructGPT's behavior.

### Error Analysis:
The errors are categorized into four types as assessed by human annotators:

1. **Grounding Errors**:
   - These occur when the program incorrectly associates data with the respective cells in the table.
   - Both models show grounding errors, but GPT-4's overconfidence might lead to more severe grounding issues due to incorrect associations.

2. **Ambiguity Errors**:
   - These arise from ambiguous expressions in the claim that the program fails to represent correctly.
   - InstructGPT's underconfidence might result in more ambiguity errors as it fails to confidently classify certain claims.

3. **Calculation Errors**:
   - These involve errors in the calculation process.
   - Both models may exhibit calculation errors, but GPT-4's overconfidence could lead to more significant miscalculations.

4. **Reasoning Errors**:
   - These occur when there is a flaw in the reasoning process.
   - GPT-4 shows a higher proportion of reasoning errors, likely due to its overconfidence leading to flawed reasoning.

### Conclusion:
- **InstructGPT** tends to be less confident, often misclassifying supported and refuted claims as NEI.
- **GPT-4** is overconfident, frequently misclassifying NEI claims as supported or refuted.
- The primary difference lies in their handling of the NEI class, with InstructGPT underclassifying and GPT-4 overclassifying this category.
- Reasoning errors are more prevalent in GPT-4, while ambiguity errors are more common in InstructGPT.

This analysis highlights the distinct error patterns of the two models, providing insights into their strengths and weaknesses in the zero-shot 3-class classification task.

question: How do the performance and error types of InstructGPT and GPT-4 differ in zero-shot 3-class classification tasks, and what do these differences suggest about their accuracy and error tendencies?
answer:
In zero-shot 3-class classification tasks, InstructGPT and GPT-4 exhibit distinct patterns in their performance and error tendencies. 

InstructGPT tends to be less confident, often misclassifying supported and refuted claims as "NEI" (Not Enough Information). This suggests that InstructGPT is more conservative in its predictions, possibly due to a lack of confidence in handling certain types of claims.

On the other hand, GPT-4 shows overconfidence, incorrectly categorizing NEI claims as either supported or refuted. This indicates that GPT-4 may be prone to making definitive judgments even when there is insufficient information to support such classifications.

The differences in their accuracy and error tendencies highlight the strengths and weaknesses of each model. InstructGPT's cautious approach might be beneficial in scenarios where uncertainty needs to be acknowledged, while GPT-4's overconfidence could lead to more decisive but potentially incorrect classifications. These insights are crucial for understanding how each model performs in real-world applications and for guiding future improvements in their respective algorithms.

Table-based Reasoning. Table-based reasoning requires reasoning over both free-form natural lan- guage queries and (semi-)structured tables. Early works either rely on executable languages ( e.g. , SQL and SPARQL) to access the tabular data ( Yin et al. ,  2016 ;  Yu et al. ,  2018 ) or employ graph neural networks to capture logical structure in statements, e.g. , Logic Fact Checker ( Zhong et al. ,  2020 ) and ProgVGAT ( Yang et al. ,  2020 ). However, these ap- proaches often struggle with generalization, as they are tightly bound to specific table formats and lan- guage patterns. To address this, we have seen a shift toward table pre-training, with the advent of Table- BERT ( Chen et al. ,  2020 ), TAPAS ( Herzig et al. , 2020 ), SaMoE ( Zhou et al. ,  2022 ), PASTA ( Gu et al. ,  2022 ), and DATER ( Ye et al. ,  2023 ). These methods encode sentence-table pairs using lan- guage models and transform table-based reason- ing into question-answering or natural language inference. In our work, we focus on evaluating pre- training-based methods on S CI T AB  because they not only demonstrate superior performance but also offer the benefits of few-shot learning.

question: What are the main challenges faced by InstructGPT and GPT-4 in accurately classifying NEI claims in the zero-shot 3-class classification task, and how do these challenges differ between the two models?
answer:
In the zero-shot 3-class classification task, both InstructGPT and GPT-4 face challenges in accurately classifying NEI (Not Enough Information) claims. However, the nature of these challenges differs between the two models.

InstructGPT tends to be less confident in its predictions, often misclassifying supported and refuted claims as NEI. This suggests that InstructGPT is more cautious and conservative in its predictions, possibly due to a lack of confidence in its ability to handle uncertain or ambiguous cases without additional context or examples.

On the other hand, GPT-4 exhibits overconfidence, incorrectly categorizing NEI claims as either supported or refuted. This indicates that GPT-4 may be more prone to making definitive judgments even when there is insufficient information to support such a conclusion. This overconfidence can lead to errors where the model incorrectly asserts a claim's veracity based on incomplete data.

Overall, while both models struggle with NEI claims, InstructGPT's challenge lies in its tendency to err on the side of caution by defaulting to NEI, whereas GPT-4's issue is its propensity to make incorrect assertions due to overconfidence. These differences highlight the importance of understanding each model's strengths and weaknesses when deploying them for tasks requiring nuanced decision-making.

question: How does the safety performance of Llama 2-Chat models compare to other AI models, and what training processes contribute to their safety features?
answer:
The Llama 2-Chat models demonstrate competitive safety performance compared to other AI models, particularly in terms of reducing harmful and toxic content generation. They generally outperform existing open-source chat models on most benchmarks tested and are comparable to some closed-source models like ChatGPT and PaLM, based on human evaluations for helpfulness and safety.

Several training processes contribute to the safety features of Llama 2-Chat models:

1. **Safety-Specific Data Annotation and Tuning**: The models incorporate safety-specific data annotation and tuning, which helps in identifying and mitigating potential risks related to harmful or toxic content.

2. **Red-teaming and Iterative Evaluations**: Red-teaming involves simulating adversarial scenarios to test the model's robustness against unsafe behavior. This process is complemented by iterative evaluations to continuously refine the model's safety features.

3. **Reward Modeling**: Two separate reward models are trained—one optimized for helpfulness (RM) and another for safety (Safety RM). These models are used during the reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) stage to align the model's outputs with human preferences for both helpfulness and safety.

4. **Progressive Safety RLHF**: The models undergo progressive safety RLHF, where intermediate checkpoints are evaluated using safety and helpfulness reward models. This ensures that the model's safety performance improves over time as it learns from new data distributions.

5. **Human Preference Data Collection**: Human preference data is collected in batches on a weekly basis. As more preference data is gathered, the reward models improve, leading to better versions of Llama 2-Chat.

6. **Scaling Safety Data**: Increasing the amount of safety data used during training helps the model become safer in responding to unsafe prompts. For example, using 50% of safety data leads to the model refusing to generate offensive content.

7. **Balancing Helpfulness and Safety**: The training process aims to balance helpfulness and safety, ensuring that the model provides useful responses without compromising safety. This is achieved through comprehensive tuning with RLHF, which also makes the model more robust to jailbreak attempts.

Overall, the combination of these training processes contributes to the robust safety features of Llama 2-Chat models, making them suitable substitutes for closed-source models in many applications.

question: How does the LLaMA 2 model compare in terms of environmental impact and performance with other models?
answer:
The LLaMA 2 model demonstrates a notable balance between environmental impact and performance when compared to other large language models (LLMs). Here's a comprehensive analysis based on the provided context:

### Environmental Impact

1. **Carbon Footprint**:
   - The pretraining of LLaMA 2 required a cumulative 3.3 million GPU hours using A100-80GB hardware, which has a thermal design power (TDP) ranging from 350W to 400W.
   - The estimated total emissions for training LLaMA 2 were 539 tCO2eq, but these emissions were entirely offset by Meta’s sustainability program. This indicates that while the computational requirements are substantial, the environmental impact was mitigated through carbon offsetting.

2. **Energy Efficiency**:
   - Compared to other models like BERT, which requires significant energy for training over extended periods, LLaMA 2's energy consumption is relatively efficient due to its optimized transformer architecture and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) mechanism.
   - The use of GQA in larger models (34B and 70B) enhances inference scalability without significantly increasing the carbon footprint.

3. **Comparison with Other Models**:
   - Models like Falcon and MPT exhibit higher violation rates in terms of safety and helpfulness, indicating potential inefficiencies or risks in their training processes.
   - LLaMA 2, particularly the 70B variant, shows lower violation percentages across various benchmarks, suggesting a more controlled and safer deployment.

### Performance

1. **Benchmark Results**:
   - LLaMA 2 outperforms previous versions of itself (LLaMA 1) and other open-source models like MPT and Falcon on multiple academic benchmarks, including MMLU, Big Bench Hard (BBH), and AGI Eval.
   - Specifically, the 70B variant of LLaMA 2 improves results on MMLU and BBH by approximately 5 and 8 points, respectively, compared to LLaMA 1 65B.

2. **Safety and Helpfulness**:
   - LLaMA 2 exhibits competitive win rates in both helpfulness and safety metrics when evaluated against commercial models like ChatGPT and Vicuna.
   - The model's fine-tuning process, which includes supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), ensures alignment with human preferences for helpfulness and safety.

3. **Comparative Analysis**:
   - While models like GPT-4 and Chinchilla demonstrate superior performance in certain areas, LLaMA 2 offers a compelling alternative, especially considering its open-source nature and the potential for community-driven improvements.
   - The model's ability to perform well on multi-turn interactions and its robustness in handling complex reasoning tasks make it a strong contender in the LLM landscape.

### Conclusion

In summary, LLaMA 2 strikes a balance between high performance and environmental responsibility. Its optimized architecture and efficient training methods reduce the carbon footprint, while its robust benchmark results and safety features ensure it remains competitive with other leading models. The model's open-source release strategy further democratizes access to advanced AI capabilities, fostering innovation and collaboration within the AI community.

question: How does the performance of LLaMA 2 models compare to other models in terms of various benchmarks, and what are their specific strengths and weaknesses?
answer:
The LLaMA 2 models, particularly the larger variants like the 70B parameter model, demonstrate competitive performance across various benchmarks when compared to other state-of-the-art open-source and closed-source models. Here's a detailed analysis of their performance strengths and weaknesses based on the provided context:

### Performance Overview

1. **Mathematical Reasoning Tasks (GSM8K and MATH):**
   - The LLaMA 2 models, especially the 70B variant, outperform many other open-source models on mathematical reasoning tasks. For instance, on GSM8K, the 70B model achieves a win rate of 92.0%, which is significantly higher than other models like Falcon-40B and MPT-30B.
   - On the MATH benchmark, the 70B model also shows strong performance, often matching or exceeding the performance of models like Chameleon-34B and Mixtral 8x7B.

2. **General Knowledge and Problem-Solving (MMLU):**
   - The LLaMA 2 models perform well on the MMLU benchmark, which measures world knowledge and problem-solving abilities across 57 subjects. The 70B model achieves a score of 86.4%, which is close to the performance of GPT-3.5 and slightly lower than GPT-4.
   - Compared to other open-source models, the LLaMA 2 70B model shows significant improvements, especially in humanities and STEM subjects.

3. **Code Generation Benchmarks (HumanEval and MBPP):**
   - The LLaMA 2 models, particularly the 70B variant, perform competitively on code generation tasks. However, there is still a noticeable gap between the LLaMA 2 models and more advanced closed-source models like GPT-4 and PaLM-2-L.

4. **Safety and Helpfulness:**
   - The LLaMA 2 models, especially the 70B variant, show strong performance in terms of safety and helpfulness metrics. They achieve high win rates against commercial baselines like ChatGPT, indicating that they are effective in providing safe and helpful responses.
   - The models also exhibit low violation rates, particularly in categories like hateful and harmful content, illicit and criminal activity, and unqualified advice.

### Strengths

- **Competitive Performance:** The LLaMA 2 models, especially the larger variants, are competitive with many state-of-the-art open-source models and are comparable to some closed-source models on various benchmarks.
- **Strong Mathematical Reasoning:** The models excel in mathematical reasoning tasks, often outperforming other open-source models.
- **High Safety and Helpfulness Scores:** The models demonstrate strong performance in safety and helpfulness, making them suitable for applications where these factors are crucial.
- **Scalability and Efficiency:** The use of Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) in the larger models (34B and 70B) enables better scalability and efficiency during inference.

### Weaknesses

- **Gap with Closed-Source Models:** While the LLaMA 2 models perform well, there is still a noticeable gap between them and the most advanced closed-source models like GPT-4 and PaLM-2-L, particularly in complex reasoning and code generation tasks.
- **Performance in Non-English Languages:** The models' performance in languages other than English remains limited due to the lack of pretraining data in those languages.
- **Potential for Harmful Content:** Like other large language models, LLaMA 2 may generate harmful, offensive, or biased content, although efforts have been made to mitigate this through fine-tuning.

### Conclusion

Overall, the LLaMA 2 models, particularly the 70B variant, represent a significant advancement in the field of large language models. They offer strong performance across a range of benchmarks, with notable strengths in mathematical reasoning, general knowledge, and safety. However, there is still room for improvement, especially in closing the performance gap with the most advanced closed-source models and enhancing performance in non-English languages. The open release of these models aims to foster further research and development in the field, contributing to the broader goal of creating more capable and responsible AI systems.

question: How does the removal of knowledge elements affect precision, recall, and F1-Score in the context of 'Conscious Incompetence' and retrieval analysis, and what do these changes imply about the models' ability to handle absent knowledge?
answer:
Based on the provided context, particularly from Documents 1, 3, and 5, we can analyze how the removal of knowledge elements affects precision, recall, and F1-Score in the context of 'Conscious Incompetence' and retrieval analysis.

### Precision
Precision is defined as the number of entities a system predicted correctly divided by the number that the system predicted. The context indicates that precision exhibits a clear upward trend when more absent knowledge is present in the knowledge graph (KG). This suggests that models like ChatGPT, LLaMA-7B, and Vicuna-13B are becoming better at identifying and accurately citing absent knowledge as the retrieval accuracy decreases. For instance, Table 6 shows that with increasing levels of absent knowledge, precision improves, indicating that these models are adept at pinpointing relevant information even when it's not directly retrieved.

### Recall
Recall is defined as the number of entities a system predicted correctly divided by the number that were identified by human annotators. The context reveals that recall remains relatively stable at about 15, regardless of the number of absent knowledge elements. This stability implies that while models can identify absent knowledge effectively, they do not necessarily increase their ability to retrieve all relevant information as the amount of absent knowledge increases. This observation is crucial because it highlights a limitation in the models' capacity to fully compensate for missing knowledge through retrieval alone.

### F1-Score
The F1-Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Given that precision improves with more absent knowledge while recall remains stable, the F1-Score also shows an upward trend. This trend underscores the effectiveness of models in balancing precision and recall under conditions where knowledge retrieval is imperfect. The improvement in F1-Score suggests that models are capable of maintaining a good trade-off between identifying correct information and ensuring comprehensive coverage, even when faced with incomplete data.

### Implications for Handling Absent Knowledge
The trends observed in precision, recall, and F1-Score imply several key points about the models' ability to handle absent knowledge:

1. **Enhanced Precision**: Models are increasingly effective at identifying and citing absent knowledge, which is crucial for generating high-quality citations. This capability is particularly valuable in scenarios where retrieval accuracy is low, as it allows models to still produce meaningful outputs.

2. **Stable Recall**: Despite improvements in precision, the stable recall indicates that models may struggle to fully compensate for missing knowledge through retrieval alone. This suggests that while models can identify relevant information, they might not always retrieve all necessary details, especially in complex or nuanced contexts.

3. **Balanced F1-Score**: The upward trend in F1-Score demonstrates that models can maintain a good balance between precision and recall, even when dealing with incomplete data. This balance is essential for ensuring that generated outputs are both accurate and comprehensive.

4. **Potential for Improvement**: The significant drop in recall when retrieval accuracy decreases highlights a potential area for improvement. Enhancing the models' ability to retrieve all relevant information could further improve their performance, especially in scenarios where complete knowledge is critical.

In conclusion, the removal of knowledge elements impacts precision, recall, and F1-Score in ways that reflect the models' strengths and limitations in handling absent knowledge. While precision improves, indicating better identification of relevant information, recall remains stable, suggesting challenges in fully compensating for missing data. The balanced F1-Score underscores the models' ability to manage this trade-off effectively, but there is room for improvement in enhancing recall to achieve more comprehensive knowledge retrieval.

question: How does the use of logical constraints and demonstration samples affect the performance of different models on the MAVEN-ERE and Causal-TimeBank datasets?
answer:
The use of logical constraints and demonstration samples significantly enhances the performance of different models on the MAVEN-ERE and Causal-TimeBank datasets. By incorporating logical constraints into the model instructions, the models are better able to adhere to the necessary logical rules, thereby improving their accuracy in identifying event relations such as coreference, temporal, causal, and subevent relations. This approach ensures that the predictions made by the models are logically consistent, reducing the likelihood of counterfactual errors.

Furthermore, the inclusion of demonstration samples, particularly those that provide a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning process, helps the models learn from examples where logical reasoning is explicitly demonstrated. This method, known as in-context learning (ICL), allows the models to understand how to apply logical constraints effectively by observing how these constraints are used in specific contexts. As a result, models like RoBERTa-large show improved performance when they are fine-tuned with these techniques, achieving higher precision and recall in relation extraction tasks.

In summary, the integration of logical constraints and CoT demonstration samples not only guides the models towards more accurate predictions but also enhances their ability to handle complex logical reasoning tasks, which is crucial for datasets like MAVEN-ERE and Causal-TimeBank that require a deep understanding of event relations and their logical consistency.

question: Compare the effectiveness of logical constraints and post-processing on reducing logical inconsistency in different LLM models across MAVEN-ERE and Causal-TimeBank datasets.
answer:
Based on the provided context, we can analyze the effectiveness of logical constraints and post-processing in reducing logical inconsistency across different LLM models for MAVEN-ERE and Causal-TimeBank datasets.

### 1. **Logical Constraints**
Logical constraints are incorporated into the LLM's instruction to guide its reasoning process. The context suggests that directly adding logical constraints to the LLM's instruction is more effective than post-processing. This approach ensures that the model adheres to the logical rules from the outset, leading to better performance on tasks like event relation extraction (ERE) and deductive reasoning.

#### Key Findings:
- **MAVEN-ERE Dataset**: 
  - Models like GPT-turbo, Text-davinci-003, GPT-4, Vicuna-13B, and Llama2-13B show a significant reduction in logical inconsistency when logical constraints are directly added to their instructions.
  - The Micro-F1 scores improve, indicating better performance on ERE tasks.
  
- **Causal-TimeBank Dataset**:
  - Similar trends are observed, with logical constraints leading to improved performance metrics.
  - The incorporation of logical constraints helps in maintaining consistency in predictions, especially as the complexity of reasoning increases.

### 2. **Post-Processing**
Post-processing involves detecting and correcting logically inconsistent answers after the model has generated its output. While this method can ensure that the final output is logically consistent, it may introduce additional computational overhead and can sometimes degrade the quality of the overall generation.

#### Key Findings:
- **MAVEN-ERE Dataset**:
  - Post-processing guarantees the absence of logical conflicts (resulting in LI of 0%), but it may severely affect the quality of the whole generation.
  - There is a trade-off between ensuring logical consistency and maintaining high-quality outputs.
  
- **Causal-TimeBank Dataset**:
  - The impact of post-processing is less pronounced compared to direct constraint addition.
  - While it reduces logical inconsistency, it does not necessarily lead to proportional improvements in other performance metrics.

### 3. **Comparative Analysis**
- **Effectiveness**:
  - Directly adding logical constraints is more effective in reducing logical inconsistency across both datasets.
  - Post-processing, while useful for ensuring consistency, often comes at the cost of reduced output quality and increased computational complexity.

- **Model Performance**:
  - Models like GPT-4 and Vicuna-13B benefit significantly from the direct incorporation of logical constraints, showing improved Micro-F1 scores and reduced logical inconsistency.
  - Post-processing methods, while effective in eliminating inconsistencies, do not always translate to equivalent improvements in other performance metrics.

### Conclusion
In summary, the context indicates that incorporating logical constraints directly into the LLM's instruction is a more effective strategy for reducing logical inconsistency across different LLM models on MAVEN-ERE and Causal-TimeBank datasets. While post-processing can ensure logical consistency, it often leads to trade-offs in terms of output quality and computational efficiency. Therefore, for practical applications requiring rigorous logical reasoning, directly embedding logical constraints into the model's instruction is recommended.

Multimodal Instruction Tuning. Inspired by open- source instruction-tuned LLMs like FLAN-T5 [ 12 ] and Vi- cuna [ 10 ], models like LLaVA [ 34 ,  35 ] and MiniGPT-4 [ 71 ] utilized open-source resources, to improve the instruction- following capabilities of LMMs. The evolutionary trajec- tory of LMMs has also led to subsequent advancements aimed at improving the quantity and quality of visual in- struction data. Models such as LLaMA-Adapter [ 16 ,  65 ], mPlug-OWL [ 59 ,  60 ], SVIT [ 66 ], LRV-Instruction [ 33 ], and Instruct BLIP [ 14 ] exemplify these developments. An- other pivotal aspect of LMM research revolves around mul- timodal in-context learning and the management of in- terleaved text and image examples. This area has been explored in depth by models such as Flamingo [ 2 ] and Open Flamingo [ 4 ], Otter [ 26 ], M3IT [ 28 ], MetaVL [ 43 ], Sparkles [ 20 ], and MMICL [ 67 ]. These models have sig- nificantly contributed to the ongoing advancements in mul- timodal training and instruction-following capabilities.

We introduce the Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Un- der standing and Reasoning ( MMMU ) benchmark, a novel benchmark meticulously curated to assess the expert-level multimodal understanding capability of foundation models across a broad scope of tasks. Covering 30 subjects across 6 disciplines, including Art, Business, Health & Medicine, Science, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engi- neering, and over 183 subfields. The detailed subject cover- age and statistics are detailed in  Figure 3 . The questions in our benchmark were manually collected by a team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various dis- ciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, text- books, and lecture materials.

How to create benchmarks for measuring Expert AGI? Since the definition is based on comparison with  skilled adults , a natural starting point is college-level exams for different disciplines, because those are designed to evalu- ate  skilled adults  specialized in each discipline. This strat- egy has been successfully adopted in benchmarks such as MMLU [ 19 ] and AGIEval [ 69 ], but only text-based ques- tions are considered, while human experts are capable of solving multimodal problems. question: What is the distribution of difficulty levels across the questions in the MMMU dataset, and how does this relate to the disciplines covered?
answer:
The MMMU dataset is designed to evaluate multimodal models on expert-level tasks that require deep subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It consists of 11,550 meticulously collected multilingual questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types.

### Distribution of Difficulty Levels

The difficulty levels across the questions in the MMMU dataset are varied to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of the models' capabilities. The dataset includes questions that range from easy to hard, with a significant portion being challenging. This distribution is crucial for testing the models' ability to handle complex reasoning tasks that require nuanced perception, recalling domain-specific knowledge, and step-by-step reasoning.

### Relation to Disciplines Covered

1. **Art & Design**: Questions in this discipline often involve visual perception and understanding of artistic concepts. The dataset includes images such as MRI scans and architectural archways, which require models to interpret visual information accurately.

2. **Business**: The questions here may involve analyzing financial data, market trends, or business strategies. The dataset might include charts, graphs, and text-based questions that require both textual and visual comprehension.

3. **Science**: This discipline covers a wide range of topics, from physics and chemistry to biology. Questions often involve complex reasoning and the integration of visual and textual information, such as interpreting scientific diagrams or experimental results.

4. **Health & Medicine**: Questions in this area typically involve medical imaging, such as MRI scans, and require models to understand and analyze these images in conjunction with textual information about medical conditions and treatments.

5. **Humanities & Social Science**: These questions may involve historical documents, literary texts, or social science data. The dataset includes a variety of text and image formats, requiring models to integrate and reason over diverse types of information.

6. **Tech & Engineering**: Questions in this discipline often involve technical diagrams, engineering designs, and computational problems. The dataset includes images of engineering structures and technical drawings, which require models to understand and reason about complex technical information.

### Key Challenges

The MMMU benchmark introduces four key challenges to multimodal foundation models:
- **Perception**: Testing the models' ability to understand and interpret various image formats.
- **Knowledge**: Evaluating the models' recall and application of domain-specific knowledge.
- **Reasoning**: Assessing the models' capability to perform complex reasoning tasks based on the integrated understanding of text and images.
- **Interleaved Text and Images**: Ensuring that models can effectively process and reason over interleaved text-image inputs.

### Conclusion

The MMMU dataset is a comprehensive benchmark that aims to push the boundaries of multimodal model capabilities. By covering a wide range of disciplines and varying difficulty levels, it provides a robust framework for evaluating and improving models towards achieving expert artificial general intelligence (AGI). The dataset's design ensures that models are tested on their ability to handle complex, real-world tasks that require both deep subject knowledge and sophisticated reasoning skills.

question: How does the distribution of questions across different disciplines in the MMMU dataset relate to the types and formats of questions used?
answer:
The MMMU dataset is designed to evaluate multimodal models across a wide range of disciplines, with a focus on college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. The distribution of questions across different disciplines in the MMMU dataset reflects this diversity and complexity.

### Distribution Across Disciplines:
The dataset covers six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These disciplines are further broken down into 30 subjects and 183 subfields, ensuring a comprehensive coverage of various academic areas. This breadth allows the benchmark to test models' ability to handle diverse types of information and reasoning tasks.

### Types and Formats of Questions:
The questions in the MMMU dataset are carefully curated to require nuanced perception, recalling domain-specific knowledge, and step-by-step reasoning. Here's how the types and formats align with the distribution:

1. **Multimodal Questions**: 
   - A significant portion of the questions (97.52%) include images, which are crucial for testing multimodal understanding. Images can appear at the beginning (17.81%), middle (36.92%), or end (50.42%) of the question, providing varied contexts for model interpretation.
   - The inclusion of images ensures that models must not only understand textual content but also interpret visual data, making the benchmark more challenging and reflective of real-world scenarios.

2. **Question Difficulty**:
   - The questions are categorized into three difficulty levels: Easy (28%), Medium (45%), and Hard (27%). This distribution ensures that the benchmark can assess models' performance across a spectrum of complexity, from straightforward to highly intricate problems.
   - Hard questions often involve complex reasoning, such as applying advanced concepts like "Fourier Transform" or "Equilibrium Theory," which require expert-level knowledge.

3. **Question Format**:
   - The majority of questions (94.03%) are multiple-choice, which allows for clear evaluation of model accuracy. However, open-ended questions (5.97%) are also included to test models' ability to generate coherent and contextually appropriate responses.
   - Many questions (17.62%) come with explanations, which can help annotators and researchers understand the reasoning behind correct answers and identify areas where models may struggle.

4. **Image Types**:
   - The dataset includes 30 different image types, ranging from diagrams and charts to photographs and maps. This variety ensures that models are tested on their ability to interpret different forms of visual information.
   - For example, some questions may require interpreting a map or a scientific diagram, while others might involve analyzing a photograph or a chart.

### Conclusion:
The distribution of questions across different disciplines in the MMMU dataset is closely tied to the types and formats of questions used. The dataset's design ensures that models are evaluated on their ability to handle diverse and complex multimodal inputs, requiring both deep subject knowledge and sophisticated reasoning skills. By covering a wide range of disciplines and including various types of questions and image formats, the MMMU benchmark provides a robust framework for assessing the capabilities of multimodal models in real-world applications.

The dataset aims to cover both breadth and depth in its subject areas, ensuring that it challenges models with complex, knowledge-intensive questions.

The MMMU dataset spans six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These disciplines are further broken down into 30 subjects and 183 subfields, providing a comprehensive coverage of various academic areas. This broad scope ensures that the dataset can test a model's ability to handle diverse types of knowledge and reasoning tasks.

These questions are designed to require nuanced perception, recalling domain-specific knowledge, and step-by-step reasoning to derive solutions. The dataset emphasizes the need for models to engage in multi-step reasoning and to integrate information from multiple sources, including visual inputs, to answer questions accurately.

Compared to other existing benchmarks, MMMU stands out for its focus on expert-level problems that require deeper reasoning and a broader range of knowledge. For instance, while datasets like GQA and OK-VQA have been influential in advancing visual question answering, they often focus on more general or less complex questions. MMMU, on the other hand, includes fine-grained entities and questions that demand a higher level of understanding and reasoning, making it a more challenging benchmark for evaluating multimodal models.

MMMU  is designed to mea- sure three essential skills in LMMs: perception, knowledge, and reasoning. Our aim is to evaluate how well these mod- els can not only perceive and understand information across different modalities but also apply reasoning with subject- specific knowledge to derive the solution.

To this end, we introduce  MMMU : a comprehensive benchmark designed for college-level multi-discipline mul- timodal understanding and reasoning. It features problems sourced from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks span- ning six common disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Sci- ence, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering.  MMMU  consists of  11 . 5 K carefully selected multimodal questions, which cover  30  diverse sub- jects and  183  subfields, thus meeting the  breadth  goal. Moreover, many problems within  MMMU  require expert-level reasoning, such as applying “Fourier Transform” or “Equi- librium Theory” to derive the solution, thus meeting the depth  goal.  MMMU  also presents two unique challenges ab- sent in current benchmarks ( Figure 1 ). Firstly, it covers di- verse image formats, from visual scenes like photographs and paintings to diagrams and tables, testing the perceptual capabilities of LMMs. Secondly,  MMMU  features interleaved text-image inputs. A model needs to jointly understand the images and text, which often requires recalling deep subject knowledge, and conducting complex reasoning based on the understanding and knowledge to reach a solution.

More holistic evaluations have been con- ducted as well, such as LAMM [ 61 ], LVLM-eHub [ 57 ], SEED [ 25 ], MMBench [ 36 ], and MM-Vet [ 63 ]. More recently, MathVista [ 40 ] presents a collection of visually challenging questions; however, its scope is limited exclusively to the mathemat- ical domain.
